title: The foot measures the shoe
hookLine: the body is the measure of what you need, as the foot is of the shoe (Enchiridion 39)

cards: Open a closet and count the shoes. Not to judge. Just count.
Then count your feet. Two, for most people. Somewhere between those two numbers there's a story.
A pair for running. Then a nicer pair for running. Then a pair that matches the jacket.
Epictetus, who by tradition lived with very little, looked at the humble shoe and saw a whole philosophy of having. Section thirty-nine is short.

teach.h: THE BODY IS THE MEASURE OF HAVING.
teach.b: The body, Epictetus says, is the measure of what each person needs to own, as the foot is the measure of the shoe. A shoe has a job, and the foot tells you when it's done.
Food, clothing, shelter: the body tells you, roughly, how much is enough. Stop there, he says, and you'll keep the measure.
Step past it, and you'll be carried along as if over a cliff. Past the measure, there's no natural place to stop. He tells the slide with a shoe.
Once you go beyond what the foot needs, the shoe becomes gilded, then purple, then embroidered. Hear the ladder in those three words: plain leather becomes a show.

teach.h: THE BODY KNOWS ENOUGH; DESIRE DOESN'T.
teach.b: Each step makes sense once you've taken the one before it, and nothing on the ladder ever says that's enough. Why is the body such a good measure? It comes with you.
It doesn't read advertisements. It gets full, it gets warm, it gets dry, and then it's done.
Desire has no such signal. Epicurus, who led a rival school, made a similar point in his own way: what nature needs is limited and easy to get, while what empty opinion wants has no limit.
Two schools, each with its own reasons, pointing at the same quiet fact. Enough is a real thing.

how: Some people practicing Stoicism use the body's actual needs as a measure for buying and owning, and notice when a want has gone past what the body asks for.

o: a rival teacher: what nature needs is limited and easy to get
a Greek teacher who praised fine food and endless luxury
the founder of the Stoic school Epictetus belonged to

games.q: the foot measures — tap the pairs.
p: the measure of what you own

s: Epictetus says a person should own nothing at all
the body is the measure: what it needs, it should have.
Epictetus says that past the measure, there's a natural place to stop
once past the measure, he says, there's no limit at all.
Epicurus, of a rival school, also said nature's needs are limited
what nature needs is limited and easy to get; empty wants have no limit.

games.q: your running shoes work fine, but a gold-trimmed pair is on sale. what would Enchiridion 39 ask?
o: ask whether the foot needs them, or the slide has begun.
games.why: the foot is the measure of the shoe. past it, the shoe goes gilded, then purple, then embroidered, and nothing says stop.

practice: Feel your feet where they rest, the clothes on your body, the seat under you; for this minute, the body has what it needs.
Think of one thing you own more than enough of, or one thing you've been wanting that the body isn't asking for, and just notice it. Then come back to your feet, and to the plain feeling of enough.

wordCard.voice: Epicurus. The rival teacher who said what nature needs is limited and easy to get; the body is the measure of what you need to own. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: a measure. Enchiridion 39 calls the body the measure of possessions.

carryVoice: Your line: the foot measures. The foot already knows where enough is. Day three hundred seventy-four.
